This is an incredible 'experience' of a game. Very immersive and gripping story right from the get go.

Characterisation is superbly done, with regular shifts in opinion of characters based on what they may or may not have done, new information comes to light constantly and you as the PC having to delicately manage your personal opinion against what is 'right' and meting out data that will in turn mete out justice.

To some of the other critics here, when looking at the gameplay elements:

There is often frustratingly insufficient evidence to go one way or the other on conflicting information - [i]That's the point[/i]. There's an allegory here for judicial systems of all stripes, that none have perfect information, even here in the information age.
And yes, sometimes you feel the need to submit certain pieces of evidence that aren't in line with the narrative you'd like to create order to progress - [i]That's the point[/i]. I felt conflicted and frustrated as a player of this [i]game[/i]. Imagine the confliction you would have in reality if you knew facts you provide would be wilfully misinterpreted by others to serve their own agenda? To be able to balance such a fine line of generating frustration in a player against the desire to see the story through to conclusion was masterful in my opinion.

A beautiful exploration of this very deep, philosophical point - that is matched by the aesthetic and depth of information to wade through in the game.

Bravo Surprise Attack Games - Orwell sets the bar in this 'cyperpunk storyteller' that will be difficult to surpass; and I'll definitely look forward to the 'datachunk' that you provide.

This game is fantastic.  It takes the themes expressed in Orwell's 1984 and allows you to take a "big brother" role by reading through social media to decide who is responsible for a series events thought to be done by terrorists.  I was on the edge of my seat the whole time, and it also made me think about every action I took.  Did I want to mark this suspect as potentially dangerous based on an altercation she got into a long time ago?  Is this article an accurate depiction of the person she is now?  Actions like these will come back to haunt you based on the outcomes later in the game.  

Overall, my only complaint with this game is that the ending felt a little too abrupt.  The game is episodic, and the final episode was significantly shorter than every other episode.  Overall, though, I would highly recommend picking this game up.

I'm a fan of this game. While I do find that there are times where I have read something only to "discover" it later, the story is intriguing and I find the concept to be original and well executed. I recommend this game to anyone who like to delve deeply into a text-based story and solve a mystery chock full of twists and turns.

I'm torn about whether or not to recommend this game. While the story has an intriguing premise and I enjoyed learning about the different characters, I was a bit disappointed. As others have mentioned, the story is quite linear and there's no point in replaying it. If you do, you can't skip the long conversations, an element that becomes tedious and annoying. This game has great potential, but I wish it offered a greater variety of paths, endings, and choices. Another issue is that there is no way to tell what information you have to process and what information is unnecessary. For this reason, you can find yourself stuck at parts, unsure of what information you're missing to trigger the next scene. At full price, I do not recommend this game. However, if you can grab it at a discounted rate, I'd say go for it. It is an enjoyable little game that is definitely worth one playthrough, but it can be slow paced at times and there's little to no point in replaying it.

More of an interactive story than a game, which is generally not my cup of tea... but this gripped me with a vice.
It completely sucked me in, and my time with Orwell left me jumping between being some sort of investigative superman uncovering and destroying the great evils and... a babbling buffoon playing puppet master and grand inquisitioner with ill understood strings at my beck and call - all the while recoiling in horror at my pernicious burrowing into other people's lives.

One little connection between seemingly unrelated and irrelevant titbits made, and dozens of lives are irrevocably destroyed. Do you rejoice at the thought of such power?

Also, of particular interest and thought provoking for people living in the UK - and other high surveillance/monitoring nations. Big brother is always watching, but is blind to context.

Get it. Play it.

Picked up this game because it was on sale and I've made many a worse decision for $5.

Played through the entire game in a single sitting (approx 6.5 hours) without leaving my seat (this excludes the time I leapt to my feet in a surge of happiness when a follow-on attack was prevented).
The plot twists and openings as the investigation consumed me. 
Do you like mysteries? Do you like intrigue? Do you want to unravel a terrorist plot, chase down leads, and feel like you're one breakthrough away from putting all the pieces together? To understand?
Then pick up this game. It's $5. You've made thousands of worse decisions for $5. This won't be one of them.

Extended Review:

First off, I HIGHLY recommend this game for people who want a story. With the gripes that I have (written below), this game still stands extremely well- which should speak to just how good this game is. This is a story driven game with deductive/mystery reasoning being the engine.

I phrase it this way intentionally, as the major issue I have with the game is in determining what information is ESSENTIAL to progress through the story. There can be times where you feel that you have to determine to send between three or four pieces of information, end up sending them all, only to find out that you didn't notice that one page linked to another.

This situation of needing to progress, sending in numerous pieces of information, and finally getting the right one or realizing another page you missed, can heavily hinder the feeling of deduction and mystery solving. One possible solution would be to provide different color for the text that is aboslutely required to continue. Alternatively, provide us with MULTIPLE SAVES. 


Some last quality of life suggestions that I would have:

-Clicking on someone's image to bring up their profile would be a nice QOL change
-A clear indication/confirmation of what the final decision in the game is and what you're trying to accomplish with it (Could just be me though)

Orwell is an awesome game and here is why I think so (no spoilers and I won't say much about the story and storytelling, because without spoilers I can say only: I really liked it):
[list]
  [*]Like the description is saying, the first chapter explains you how to use your tools, but this is only the technical "how to use". You will have to learn a lot more and you will learn.
  [*]You, your imagination, your thoughts and your conclusions are the most important part of the game. It's feeling more like the game does what you want and not the other way arount and I really appreciate this.
  [*]You have many options to handle things right until the end. And some decisions you made earlier may have an impact on later events.
  [*]It's very immersive if you are willing to let it happen (maybe even if you're not).
  [*]There are some more intense and some calmer phases in the game but it really never felt boring. There was never a point where I was like "yeah, and now?".
  [*]If you want to take a break, you can do it every time you want to or take the offered breaks after every day. Or finish the game in one playthrough like I did ;)
  [*]The music and artstyle fit the game perfectly and the gameplay itself is simple, but that is how it should be. You will find a reason why it is how it is in the story.
[/list]
So, I really reccomend this game if you're into games which let you make decisions, have a storytelling which lets you rethink your conclusions again and again and again, get you involved if you want it or not and handle current subjects and events (in a fictional way of course).

I will definitely play it again to see what changes my decisions make.

Outstanding story driven game. The core game mechanics are very simple, mostly pouring through e-mails, texts, websites, all in the search of clues regarding a terrorist network. The information more or less is highlighted for you, so simply gathering the required information is easy. However, the player's decision to share certain pieces of information with the government can have profound impacts on the story and the characters involved. The decisions are far from black and white, often with undesired consequences. The interface is intuitive and immersive, creating a genuine impression of spying on suspected terrorists and political activists. It would be easy to assume the entire game is a critique of authoritarian government adapting "orwellian" tactics. However, theres is substantially more depth to the story. From a benevolent perspective (the player) it's easy to see how such powerful tools saves lives. Conversely, and predictably perhaps, the consequences and implications of such a system are made very apparent. The story is genuinely well written, the characters being surveilled are well fleshed out, and the mystery at the center of the plot is incredibly intriguing. There isn't much depth to the gameplay, or length for that matter (roughly 4 hrs), but it's worth playing for the story itself. This is one of those "story driven, choices matter, indie" games that genuienly earns those taglines and is well worth a playthrough. The only game I can relate it to is the similarly fantastic "papers, please". In much the same regard, this game engrosses the player in the mechanics of beurocracy, of distilling peoples lives, relationships, motivations, into government business. You'll find yourself so engrossed with the mechanics of discovering as much as possible about these people, the hidden agendas, the breadcrumbs left across blog posts and webpages, that you'll forget about their actual humanity. It would be boringly simple for the developers to phone the plot in with a simple anti-orwellian plot. They go so much deeper than that, using the player's perspective itself within the message. A truly well written game, with a genuinely innovative and engaging core mechanic.

There's social commentary that makes you think, and then there's social commentary that makes you nod. I regret to inform you that Orwell falls into the latter category. It's still worth checking out, especially if you've been living under a rock for the last 150 years.

Orwell has you play as the operator of a new surveillance system in the wake of a terror attack to catch the perpetrator(s). Starting off with a single suspect, Cassandra Watergate, you must sift through texts, emails, phone calls and websites to unravel the truth behind the attack. [b]This game is best played going in blind[/b] so I'd recommend just purchasing it now as I will spoil minor plot details. The game is very good, but not quite as good as I'd expected.

[h1][b]SPOILERS START HERE[/b][/h1]

To begin with, I read all of the information I could. The interface of Orwell is designed to pressure you into reading everything, seeming almost 'unclean' if you don't. However, the main mechanic of the game is the relevant text which is highlighted, regardless of whether or not you've read the whole page. Overall, this was a good move, but it did mean that I soon started scrolling through webpages, reading only what was highlighted.

Another game mechanic is the conflicting information system. If a piece of information conflicts something else that [i]can[/i] be read, it is highlighted in yellow and only of these pieces can be uploaded to Orwell. These are the points where the game branches, but it does not do so to a large extent and the development of characters is nothing like larger games with branching stories. Some of these pieces of conflicting information are pure guesswork, a poor choice made worse by the fact that [spoiler]a third terror attack[/spoiler] will occur if the player does not guess correctly.

The game has four endings. Because the player is not seen as much of an actual character, these endings didn't stir any emotion inside me, something that I believe could have been remidied by making the game longer. In all likelyhood, you will only see one ending because the game has a low replayability factor.

On a positive note, the music is amazing and, when you discover critical information, there is a sudden dramatic noise which I can only describe as feeling like my heart shat its pants.

I have focused on negatives in this review. Overall, the game is great fun, sends a good message and is certainly worth its price tag.
7/10 recommended

I'm also thinking a lot about the endings. 
I had to make decision between upload fake evidence to obey the order, or quit my job. I get the idea that Orwell should not exist, but I really don't like the way Thoughts members protested. I don't want to set them free. They should pay for the troubles they had made. But I don't want to use fake evidence, because investigator's job is to provide true and unbiased info as an outsider, not to manipulate the consequence, even if the consequence is good and wanted. I wish the dialog of Thoughts' last meeting is usable, so that I can upload true evidence to catch that person. Anyway, I caught Catherine instead. Orwell is an narrative game with unique gameplay. The game puts you in the shoes of an investigator whose job it is to keep the Nation safe. You work with the titular program 'Orwell' which is an advanced search engine that lets you browse the in game internet in search of terrorists. You will start of by reading through public blogs, forums and social media. But as the stakes rise and the public information dries up you will find yourself spending more and more time eavesdropping on phone calls and hacking into personal files.

The feel of the game reminds me a bit of Deus Ex. I personally loved hacking computers and reading emails in those games, and Orwell turns this side activity into a full game. This means that you will do a lot of reading, although the useable pieces of information are always highlighted. You can upload these 'data chunks' to your superior, who will act on the information you feed him. Your superior cannot read anything except for the parts you upload, which gives you the freedom to interpret the data and even 'spin' it. Do you focus on the information that marks someone as potentially dangerous or do you focus on their peaceful side? This will ofcourse have consequences down the road.

Speaking of consequences, these are actually real in this game. Although your actions will not change the core structure of the narrative, they will have a very clear impact. All suspects can be arrested, one can be killed, or you can let them all go free. What makes this game unique is that most consequences are not directly tied to a single choice, but to a whole set of smaller decisions. There is no 'do you let this person live?' moment. Instead the choices you made in what data you upload and what information you ignore will determine the fate of the characters. The ending may appear to be a 'choose your own ending' affair at first, but a replay made it clear to me that your earlier choices will still impact the ending you get.

The theme of the game is privacy vs safety. But unlike other games or media on this subject, there is no clear black or white. The game shows that your work can save lives, but that it also has the potential to ruin them. The characters constantly move between light grey and dark grey, sometimes praising violence and sometimes worrying about their family. Only in the final episode do two characters clearly turn out to be evil, but even then the game takes no position on the core debate, allowing the player the freedom to think about it themselves.

Sadly the game has a very short runtime. The first play through will take about 4-5 hours. If you skip past most text you will be done even faster. The game has some replay value, partially due to its short length, but the first play through is much more fun than the second.

There is one potential problem with this game: it is all in text. If you like reading lore, this will be fine. But if you tend to skip across text, the game will likely become boring fast. Even the phone calls are in text. Only the intro is animated. Despite this, the game can still be nail biting tense as police move in on the potential location of a bomb or terrorist and you can do little but follow the news and related phone calls, hoping that your work was enough to save the day.

Tl;dr: a great narrative game with actual choices, but lots of text. If you skipped to the tl;dr there is probably too much text for you!

Rating: 9/10

While the game mechanics may not be appealing to people—you are essentially combing through web pages and social media like profiles of different "target" characters as a cyber detective trying to gain information about them, which ultimately amounts to the same experience you would have actually surfing the web or social media sites—the storyline and scenario are EXTREMELY engaging and thought-provoking. The topics of surveillance is more relevant than ever these days, and one has to wonder if the Orwell system of hacking into other people's digital lives is not already in use in more or less the same form by the NSA and so forth.

If you are someone like me who is skeptical about the benefits of surveillance technology and who supports people like Edward Snowden's efforts of exposing the secrecy of our government, then this game will be particularly fascinating to you. The characters are interesting and feel well developed, and the developers did an amazing job packing tons of content to read and sift through, so the "world" feels fairly believable. There are tough decisions to be made and deep issues at hand here, not just about surveillance but freedom of speech, terrorism, and there are many gray areas to delve into. Nothing is ever as it appears, quite like life. Some great twists in the story as well. 


If you are looking for a thoughtful, provocative experience that gets right into the hard questions we should be thinking about these days, then I highly recommend you check out Orwell.

The story is definitely intriguing and it unfolds very nicely given the pacing. There is quite a bit of freedom as a result (ironic, huh) and while there is somewhat limited replayability, it's definitely really good at keeping the tension and suspense, some of which you may be able to find out depending on what you do or don't flag.

Although a short game (5hrs for me), Orwell sucked me in right from the start. It does start off a little slow, however the pace picks up throughout the game until the finale where you can almost feel the tension and the sense of urgency with what you're doing.

What you have instead is a fairly captivating narrative which allows you to act as a snoop and voyeur into the lives of a group of people thought to be a sinister organisation with a view to bringing people to justice.
